title.text: Ninoy Aquino Parks and Wildlife Center

title_en.text: Ninoy Aquino Parks and Wildlife Center

tagline.text: A park in the middle of Quezon City where rescued wildlife and a lagoon sit within 24 hectares of green space

location.label: Location
location.text: Corner of Quezon Avenue and Elliptical Road, Diliman, Quezon City

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱100–500 (admission, transport and snacks, per person)

children.text: The Ninoy Aquino Parks and Wildlife Center is a city park of about 24 hectares in Diliman, Quezon City, and it opened in 1970. It cares for confiscated and rescued wildlife, so you can stroll past a lagoon and under shady trees while seeing Philippine animals up close.

The Ninoy Aquino Parks and Wildlife Center is in the Diliman district of Quezon City, Metro Manila. It sits at the corner of Quezon Avenue and Elliptical Road, which means you can reach a green space of big trees and a lagoon right in the middle of the city. According to Wikipedia, the area is about 23.85 hectares (about 59 acres), and it is managed by the Biodiversity Management Bureau (BMB) under the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR). Locally it is often shortened to NAPWC, and some people still know it by its old name, the Lungsod ng Kabataan Park.

The history here is a little complicated. In 1954 the land was set aside as part of Quezon Memorial Park, and between 1968 and 1969 it was reduced to its present size. The center opened to the public on

. In 1983 it reopened as the Lungsod ng Kabataan Recreational Park, and in 1986 it took its current name in honor of the assassinated senator Benigno "Ninoy" Aquino Jr. In 2011 what had been a small zoo took on a new role as the National Wildlife Rescue and Research Center, and in 2018 the site was declared a national park under Republic Act No. 11038. Some pages on Wikipedia give 1954 as the opening date, so the years differ a little by source. The 1954 Quezon Memorial Park was created by Proclamation No. 42, and this land was a part of it. Wikipedia also explains that between 2000 and 2002 the area lost its protected-area status and then had its name restored. As the city grew, the park's character changed several times, so it is easiest to think of it as a long-standing public green space.

This is closer to a shelter for rescued wildlife than to the tourist zoo you might imagine. The animals here were confiscated in smuggling crackdowns, rescued after being hurt, or handed in after being kept as pets. Wikipedia lists crab-eating macaques, water monitors, Philippine deer, binturongs, Palawan bearded pigs and several kinds of birds, and a 2024 visitor account mentions gibbons, saltwater crocodiles, tigers, emus and a Philippine eagle. Which animals you can see changes over time, so check the official information before you go. Wikipedia notes that around 2018 the animals numbered about 1,400 and the facilities were overcrowded. So rather than expecting wide enclosures where animals run free, we suggest walking around with an understanding of the situation of animals being cared for in limited facilities. What animals are here and how many changes often, so the list in this article is for reference only.

Besides the animal areas, there are plenty of pleasant paths and resting spots. A man-made lagoon of about 4 hectares holds fish such as tilapia, carp and catfish, and there is a viewing gazebo on the shore. On one side of the lake there are stilt-house-style buildings and an open-air amphitheater that seats 500 to 600 people, and the park also has the Museum of Philippine Biodiversity, which opened in May 2017, a botanical garden and a playground. Some sources mention an elevated walkway linking the park to Quezon Memorial Circle, but check on site whether it is open now. Visitors were reported at about 300,000 in 2013. On weekends many local families and student groups come, but weekday mornings are relatively quiet and good for a peaceful walk, according to visitor accounts. Some reviews also say the facilities are old and worn. Rather than expecting a flashy amusement park, think of it as a place to walk slowly for two or three hours in the middle of Manila and look at Philippine animals, and you will likely be happier with it. The trees are a sight too. An estimate from 2012 puts the number of mature trees at about 4,500, so you walk in the kind of deep shade that is rare in Manila. Filipinos treat this place as the city's lungs and use it for morning walks and family outings.

blocks.title: National Wildlife Rescue and Research Center

children.text: This facility cares for confiscated and rescued animals. Philippine deer, crab-eating macaques, water monitors and binturongs are among the animals reported. Its purpose is protection, so do not expect hands-on contact with the animals.

A lagoon of about 4 hectares lies at the center of the park. Walking slowly once around the shore path softens the noise of the city. From the viewing gazebo you can rest and watch the birds and fish on the water.
This exhibition space opened in May 2017 and introduces the biodiversity of the Philippines. Opening hours and admission conditions may change, so ask at the ticket booth.

Sculptures on wildlife and environmental themes are scattered around the park. One reported piece, "Elephants," is made of steel mixed with ashes from elephant tusks confiscated in 2013, and at the Quezon Avenue entrance there are "Children at Play" statues.

As of 2009, the park was reported to hold thousands of tree species, about 100 of them endemic to the Philippines. There are also plants whose fruit is used medicinally, such as the tagpo, a Philippine ardisia. The shade is wide, so it stays relatively cool even at midday.
With a children's playground, picnic gazebos and an open-air amphitheater, it is a good place to visit with kids.
The park is large, so walking it slowly gives you a fair bit of exercise. It suits a half-day outing where you take your time and photograph small sights.

blocks.title: Stilt houses and amphitheater by the lagoon

children.text: On one side of the lagoon there is a fishing-village-style complex of five stilt houses, along with an open-air amphitheater that seats 500 to 600 people. Except on event days it is quiet, which makes it a nice place to rest. Check on site whether the amphitheater can be used and what events are scheduled.

items.title: Basic 2–3 hour route
items.subtitle: Enter just after opening and tour the animals and the lagoon

children.text: Enter right at opening time. Mornings are cool and easy for walking. Pay the fee at the entrance and check the map.
Start with the wildlife area. Take your time with the monkeys, deer, birds and reptiles, and read why each animal is being cared for on the signs.
Head to the lagoon, walk the shore path and rest at the viewing gazebo. This is a good time to watch the birds and fish on the water.
Visit the biodiversity museum and botanical garden, and photograph the sculptures.
Leave before the sun gets hot and have a snack or a meal on the Quezon Avenue side.

Parts of the animal area may be closed because of facility conditions. Change the order to match on-site guidance. If it is your first visit, pick up a map or take a photo of the sign at the entrance to find your way more easily. The park is large, and just going around the lagoon is a fair walk, so rest often at the gazebo if you get tired.

items.title: Quezon City half-day combination
items.subtitle: From the park to Quezon Memorial Circle

children.text: Reach the park from the Quezon Avenue MRT-3 station on foot, or by jeepney or taxi.
Tour the wildlife center.
Leave the park and head toward Quezon Memorial Circle. It is close, but you have to cross roads, so watch for traffic as you walk.
Stroll around Quezon Memorial Circle and see the memorial shrine.
Have lunch at a nearby restaurant or mall and finish there.

From the Makati or EDSA side, take the MRT-3 line and get off at Quezon Avenue station. One blog describes a walk of a few minutes from the station to the park entrance, but another guide (2024, map app) puts even the nearest MRT-3 station at about a 20-minute walk, so sources differ. Other guides tell you to take a jeepney (toward Quezon Avenue and Elliptical Road) or a taxi from the station, so check the distance on a map app before you walk.
Trains are very crowded at rush hour, so avoid those times. Check the latest announcements for service status.
You can go from Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL) by taxi or Grab. The travel time varies a lot with traffic, so leave plenty of margin.
Another option is to go first to an MRT station or a city transfer point and then change to the train.
Jeepneys and buses run along Quezon Avenue and Elliptical Road. Routes and fares change often, so check on site.
A Grab or taxi will drop you at the roadside in front of the park. Decide in advance on an easy spot to catch a ride back.
With so many outdoor facilities, the dry season with less rain is the most comfortable time to go. During the day, the morning just after opening is cool and quiet, which is good for walking.
In the rainy season, sudden downpours can wet the paths and some animals may hide. Bring an umbrella and a light raincoat.

The park is in Quezon City, so you can base yourself near Quezon City or in an area you prefer, such as Makati or BGC. Moving along the MRT-3 line keeps transport easy. You cannot stay overnight inside the park. A visit to the center alone takes about half a day, so it is efficient to add another Quezon City sight on the same day. If you are coming from central Manila, a plan to go in the morning and return before lunch works well.

There is no confirmed information about food stalls inside the park, so the restaurants along Quezon Avenue or in nearby malls give you wider choices. If you come with children, bring water and snacks, and because food brought in may be restricted under park rules, check at the entrance. Quezon City has plenty of restaurants, so it is easy to have lunch after leaving the park. For well-regarded long-running places, you can also ask in the local Korean community.

Bring water, a hat, sunscreen and an umbrella. Even with plenty of shade it is hot at midday.
You will walk a long way, so wear comfortable shoes. If you are with children, decide on resting spots in advance.
Do not feed or touch the animals. It is very stressful for rescued animals.
Parts of the animal area may be closed for maintenance. Check the latest information through the official Quezon City contacts.
Do not use a flash when taking photos.
Walking from the MRT station, you have to cross roads, so watch for traffic.
There is no confirmed information on restrooms and snack stalls inside the park, so bring water and tissues in advance.
Fees, opening hours and the state of the animal displays can change. Check the latest official and on-site information.
Watch your belongings. On the crowded MRT, wear your bag in front.
Monkeys and some other animals may snatch food or items, so do not show your bags.
Paths can be slippery in the rainy season, so be careful.
Some facilities are old and worn, and access to some areas may be limited. Follow the signs.
This is a wildlife facility, so keep the noise down and stay on the designated paths.
In animal areas, do not go close to the fences or lean on them. Hold your children's hands firmly.
A large memorial park close to the center. You can walk there, but you have to cross roads, so watch for traffic.
A forest park in the north of Quezon City, good to combine when you want more nature. We recommend a taxi or Grab to get there.
Manila's signature city park, which lets you plan a day around two city parks.
